entry.evidence: opens new avenues for studying phase relations in peridotites and other lithologies in different mantle layers

steps.action: Pose the aim of using thermodynamic modeling of KLB-1 to analyze the mineralogy of mantle layers and their boundaries during early Earth evolution.
steps.quote: to analyze the mineralogy of the various Earth’s mantle layers and boundaries between them during the early Earth’s evolution

steps.action: Design the Perple_X 6.9.0 calculation: the KLB-1 composition reduced to NCFMAS, database hp622ver.dat, chosen solid-solution models (Gt(H) chosen so that majorite can dissolve Na), and a P–T range of 0–30 GPa and 600–2000 °C.
steps.quote: The simulations for the NCFMAS system were carried out using the thermodynamic database hp622ver.dat (Holland and Powell, 2011)

steps.action: Compute the P–T phase diagram (Fig. 1), which shows a broad garnet wehrlite field in the upper mantle and a ringwoodite-free field where the slope of the lower transition-zone boundary turns positive.
steps.quote: At higher temperatures, ringwoodite is absent, and the slope of the line becomes positive (Fig. 1).

steps.action: Set the thermal conditions: modern and Archean oceanic geotherms and adiabats (Tp 1300 and 1550 °C) and a modern 45 mW/m2 continental geotherm; the Archean continental geotherm is omitted because it is too uncertain.
steps.quote: The oceanic geotherms were calculated according to (Turcotte and Schubert, 2002) for a 60-Ma plate and the modern mantle

steps.action: Compute modal abundances, pyroxene compositions and density profiles along the geotherms (Figs. 2, 3); the Archean mantle lacks ringwoodite and orthopyroxene, and its transition zone is thinner.
steps.quote: the Archean mantle at pressures above ~3 GPa contains no orthopyroxene, i.e., the mantle mineralogy corresponds to that of wehrlite.

steps.action: Check the thermodynamic model against published KLB-1 experiments (Takahashi; Zhang & Herzberg; Hirose; Matsukage & Kubo) and solidus curves; the liquidus and the wehrlite field agree, while the garnet lherzolite at 5 GPa, the Katz solidus offset and the NAl and bridgmanite occurrences are discussed as mismatches.
steps.quote: The diagram is reasonably well consistent with experimental data for composition KLB-1.

steps.action: Compare the computed diagram with the THERMOCALC diagram of Holland et al. (2013), which uses the same database: the diagrams are closely similar, garnet lherzolite boundaries and Hpx amounts differ, and both show the ringwoodite-free area.
steps.quote: Our calculated phase diagram is closely similar to that in (Holland et al., 2013, Fig. 1)

steps.action: Reproduce exactly the published Stixrude & Lithgow-Bertelloni (2011) pyrolite phase diagram in Perple_X with the stx11 database, to isolate the effect of bulk composition.
steps.quote: we first exactly reproduced the phase diagram in (Stixrude and Lithgow-Bertelloni, 2011, Fig. 16)

steps.action: Recompute the KLB-1 diagram with the alternative stx11 database (Fig. 4); it gives wehrlite-like modes with accessory Opx and a ringwoodite-free kink at ~1980 °C, higher than with hp622.
steps.quote: It is important to mention that this thermodynamic dataset also predicts that ringwoodite ceases to be stable

steps.action: Keep the two robust model predictions across databases: broad garnet wehrlite stability in the upper mantle and a ringwoodite-free transition zone at high temperature.
steps.quote: Available thermodynamic data predict major effects for the composition of spinel lherzolite KLB-1 related to the broad stability of garnet wehrlite

steps.action: Take from the literature the natural record: wehrlites are rare among orogenic, abyssal and ophiolitic peridotites and among arc and kimberlite xenoliths.
steps.quote: Wehrlites, including their garnet varieties, are relatively rare peridotite types in orogens, abyssal regions, and ophiolites (Fig. 5).

steps.action: Set the predicted widespread asthenospheric wehrlite against its rarity in natural samples and identify a paradox.
steps.quote: look like paradoxical and deserve discussion

steps.action: Protect the KLB-1 wehrlite-mantle claim with an auxiliary: samples re-equilibrate along cooler lithospheric geotherms during ascent and long conductive cooling, so they convert to lherzolite.
steps.quote: the rarity of wehrlites among mantle rocks brought to the Earth’s surface may be explained by a valuable temperature change on the geotherms

steps.action: Compute Ol–Opx–Cpx modal trajectories along continental and oceanic geotherms (Fig. 5), showing orthopyroxene growth as KLB-1 rises along continental geotherms.
steps.quote: shall be associated with an increase in the modal amount of orthopyroxene (Fig. 5)

steps.action: Discuss refining the NCFMAS model with Cr and Fe3+, using published calculations by Jennings & Holland (2015); the effects are small at the 0–30 GPa scale but matter in the shallow mantle.
steps.quote: These changes are hardly discernible in the phase diagram

steps.action: Compare the computed transition-zone boundary slopes with simple-system experiments: they agree for the upper boundary and only partly for the lower one.
steps.quote: are well consistent with data on the slope of the upper boundary but partially with the lower one.

steps.action: Derive the geodynamic consequences of the Clapeyron slopes for slabs and plumes in modern and Archean conditions (Fig. 6): a positive Archean lower-boundary slope accelerates plume ascent.
steps.quote: the onset of ringwoodite instability and ensuing change in the slope of the mantle transition zone boundary in P–T space may have stimulated mantle diapirism

steps.action: Conclude that the modeling reproduces experiments and that a KLB-1-type modern upper mantle is dominated by a garnet-wehrlite-like assemblage.
steps.quote: the modern upper mantle (if its composition is of KLB-1 type) is dominated by a mineral assemblage like that of garnet wehrlite

steps.action: Propose the 'Archean window' for lower-mantle plumes, supporting whole-mantle convection, pending experimental confirmation of the ringwoodite-free field.
steps.quote: this shall attract much attention to the topic of “Archean window” for lower-mantle plumes

tree.answer: Phase relations of KLB-1 peridotite across mantle P–T conditions up to 30 GPa
No; deep mantle mineralogy is computed by Gibbs energy minimization
Map the mineralogy of mantle layers and boundaries, modern versus Archean
No rival hypotheses; alternative thermodynamic databases and published experiments serve as references
Databases differ in the wehrlite field temperature and the ringwoodite-free kink (1820 vs ~1980 °C)
Largely: consistent with experiments, Holland et al. 2013 and the stx11 database; the ringwoodite-free field is untested experimentally
Kept: wehrlite-dominated upper mantle and ringwoodite-free field, with experimental verification called for

end.claim: For a KLB-1 composition, the convecting upper mantle is dominated by a garnet wehrlite assemblage, and a ringwoodite-free field at high temperature turns the slope of the 660-km boundary positive, crossed by Archean adiabats and hot plumes.

decisive_move.sentence: The Perple_X calculation of the KLB-1 phase diagram (Fig. 1) is the source of both the wehrlite field and the ringwoodite-free field on which all other claims rest.

gates.evidence: The phase diagram was computed without a hypothesis directing it. The claims were checked against published experiments, which could have disagreed and partly did (5 GPa garnet lherzolite, solidus offset), and against a second database. No experiments exist in the ringwoodite-free region (p. 203). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Gibbs free energy minimization to compute stable phase assemblages (Perple_X)
Clapeyron slope of phase transitions controlling buoyancy

novelty_claims.quote: reveals the peculiarities of mantle mineral assemblages at P–T parameters on which experimental data are insufficient or absent
Thermodynamic modeling reveals a ringwoodite-free field in the P–T diagram
nor related effects were discussed in (Holland et al., 2013)
was not identified in the experimental products, but our diagram predicts its occurrence

limits: Only the published paper was supplied. A reviewer (A.V. Girnis) is acknowledged, but no review file was given, so no review sequence is coded. No uncertainty is given for any computed boundary or modal abundance. The ringwoodite-free field has no experimental test (p. 203). Sub-claims: the claim that the modeling reproduces experiments is capability_characterized. The explanation of wehrlite rarity by re-equilibration during ascent is a protective auxiliary supported only by computed trajectories, at status best_explanation at most. The 'Archean window' and whole-mantle convection idea is a hypothesis with status none. The Cr and Fe3+ refinements are cited, not computed here. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a computation of a model, checked against references and alternative databases, then interpreted. It has no rivals, crucial test, trace series, or frozen forecast, and capability_first does not fit because the software and databases are not new here. The entry as capability is an inference from the introduction's framing. Whether the Holland et al. (2013) comparison counts as performed here is a coder judgment: the comparison is done here, the alternative computation is not.

disagreements.support: They reproduce the published pyrolite diagram and recompute it for KLB-1 with the same database, attributing the ~700 °C higher wehrlite field mainly to the different bulk composition.
disagreements.quote: the field of garnet wehrlite occurs at T > 2000°C, which is ~700°C higher than our estimates

disagreements.support: The computed solidus lies 20–80 °C above the Katz parameterization, the gap increasing with pressure (Fig. 1).
disagreements.quote: the calculated dry solidus of average lherzolite (Katz et al., 2003) occurs at lower temperatures than the solidus based on our data

disagreements.support: Garnet lherzolite between solidus and liquidus at 5 GPa is absent in the model; the authors argue that the published diagrams fit the model better than the tabulated assemblages.
disagreements.quote: the diagrams in (Zhang and Herzberg, 1994; Herzberg and Zhang, 1996) are much better consistent with our data than the mineral assemblages listed

disagreements.support: A wider experimental garnet lherzolite field is reinterpreted, since orthopyroxene modes were not reported and could be accessory.
disagreements.quote: this does not rule out the occurrence of the wehrlite mineral assemblage with accessory amounts of orthopyroxene

disagreements.support: General agreement is reported; NAl was not found experimentally, bridgmanite appears at transition-zone pressures, and pressures are uncertain by up to 1.2 GPa.
disagreements.quote: the boundaries between the fields are not always strictly consistent

disagreements.target: Holland et al. (2013) calculated KLB-1 phase diagram
disagreements.support: Same database but different code and upper-mantle solution models give different garnet lherzolite boundaries and much smaller Hpx amounts.
disagreements.quote: Our data indicate (Fig. 2) that high-pressure pyroxene appears in very small amounts (no more than 1 vol %)

disagreements.target: Negatively sloped ringwoodite–bridgmanite boundary from simple-system experiments (Akaogi, 2007; Bina, 1994; Hirose, 2002)
disagreements.support: In the more complex KLB-1 system the absence of ringwoodite at high temperature makes the boundary slope positive (Figs. 1, 4).
disagreements.quote: are well consistent with data on the slope of the upper boundary but partially with the lower one.

disagreements.target: Use of kimberlite peridotite xenoliths as samples of Early Precambrian mantle
disagreements.support: Computed modal trajectories along continental geotherms show wehrlite converting to lherzolite during long conductive cooling and ascent.
disagreements.quote: peridotite xenoliths from kimberlite pipes cannot strictly represent the mineral assemblages of the Early Precambrian mantle

alternatives_considered.reason: Na component of majorite not included in Grt(JH); Gt(H) applies to the upper mantle and transition zone

alternatives_considered.reason: stx11 does not include melting, so results cannot be compared with the experimental data

alternatives_considered.reason: close to primitive mantle and widely used in experiments

alternatives_considered.reason: components not included in solid-solution models
